tour.title: Harbour, Antiphellos & the Lycian Coast
tour.summary: A relaxed loop through a Lycian port town — the working harbour, a Hellenistic theatre that faces the sea, a rock-cut tomb with an unreadable poem on it, a pebble cove for a swim, and the peninsula at sunset.
tour.overviewText:
Kaş shows you its past by accident. You are walking to the bakery when a two-thousand-year-old stone coffin stands in the middle of the shopping street, lid and lions' heads and all, and nobody gives it a second look. Down at the harbour the water is so clear that the boats seem to float on their own shadows. The name on the map is Turkish; the town underneath is Lycian, Greek and Roman by turns.

The place is ancient Antiphellos — Antifellos in Turkish, "the land opposite the rocks" in Greek, and Habesos before that, in the language of the Lycians. The Lycians (Likya in Turkish) were not Greeks: they were a distinct people of south-western Anatolia with their own Indo-European language, their own alphabet adapted from Rhodes, and a habit of carving their dead into the cliffs and standing their sarcophagi in the streets. They also built one of the ancient world's first federations, the Lycian League, which gave member cities votes in proportion to their size — a design the American founders, James Madison among them, later read with interest.

Geography did the rest. Antiphellos was the harbour for Phellos, a city up in the hills, and it grew rich on trade until the inland city faded and this one became the region's largest. In 141 AD an earthquake and tsunami wrecked the Lycian coast; you meet the same fault line again if you take the boat to the sunken city at Kekova. Under the Ottomans the town was called Andifli, and most of its people were Greek Orthodox. Then in 1923, after the Greco-Turkish war, Greece and Turkey agreed at Lausanne to a compulsory exchange of populations sorted by religion: about 1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians left Turkey, and some 355,000 to 400,000 Muslims left Greece. Andifli's Greek community went to Greece; Muslims from Greece moved into their houses. Two kilometres offshore, the Greek island of Kastellorizo — Meis in Turkish — stayed Greek, because Italy then held it. That is why the lights across the water belong to another country. State it plainly: neither community chose this; the two governments did.

Today the town earns its living from the sea differently. Sponge-diving and fishing gave way to tourism: dive schools working some fifty sites, sea-kayak trips to the Kekova sunken city, boat days along the coast, and a long-distance footpath, the Lycian Way, that passes through town — a separate expedition, not this afternoon's. The walk here is deliberately easy. It starts on the harbour, climbs to a Hellenistic theatre that faces the sea, drops into the shopping lanes to a Lycian tomb, comes down to a pebble cove for a swim, then crosses to the peninsula for sunset and returns along the waterfront. It is short, and it is meant to be walked slowly.

Almost all of it is free — the theatre, the tomb and the coves cost nothing, though sunbeds, boat trips and the ferry to Meis do. Bring Turkish lira, the currency written ₺, for the dolmuş and the tea, and verify any price at the gate or with the driver — prices move. Late September is close to perfect here: warm sea, softer light, thinner crowds.

Start at the harbour. The whole town is in front of you.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Mostly level waterfront and lanes, with one short stepped climb to the theatre and a gentle walk out along the peninsula. Surfaces are cobbled, uneven and sometimes slick after rain, and the theatre's stone rows are worn and steep.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start mid-afternoon, around 3 to 4pm, so you reach the theatre in good light, swim while the sea is still warm, and are on the peninsula for the hour before sunset. The walk then finishes at the harbour front as the restaurants light up. Mornings are cooler and quieter, but the peninsula show is an evening one.

stops.name: Kaş Harbour
stops.narration:
You are standing at the liman — the harbour — which is the reason this town exists at all. Everything in front of you is a working sea: wooden gulets, the two-masted sailing boats that carry day-trippers out to the islands; dive boats stacked with tanks, because Kaş is one of Turkey's diving capitals; and a few small fishing boats that are the last echo of the old economy. Gület is the Turkish name for those wooden boats — the type was built for cargo and sponge fishing, and now it carries tourists instead.

Look at the water. It is unnaturally clear, and there is a reason. This coast is limestone, with almost no large rivers to wash silt into the sea, so there is very little for algae to feed on and almost nothing suspended in the water. That clarity is what makes the diving here — some fifty sites within reach, including six deliberately sunk wrecks used as artificial reefs, a Second World War aircraft and a 1950s cargo ship. It is also what made this bay worth holding for well over two thousand years.

The old town under your feet is Antiphellos, "the land opposite the rocks", the harbour for Phellos, a city up in the hills behind you. Ancient Antiphellos had no city wall and no acropolis — unusual for its age — because the sea and a natural reef did the defending. It minted its own coins and, as the inland city declined, grew into the region's biggest port. The geographer Strabo, writing in Greek in the first century, got it wrong and listed Antiphellos as an inland town; the sailors' guidebooks knew better.

Now look south, out to sea. That island about two kilometres away is Kastellorizo — Meis in Turkish, Megisti in Greek, meaning "the greatest", which is a joke, since it is the smallest inhabited island of the Greek Dodecanese. It is Greek, and it is closer to this quay than most of Turkey is. Before 1923 the water between here and there was not a border at all: the town was called Andifli, most of its people were Greek Orthodox, and families crossed back and forth to tend vineyards and buy at market. After the Greco-Turkish war, Greece and Turkey agreed at Lausanne in 1923 to exchange populations by religion — roughly 1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians out of Turkey, and 355,000 to 400,000 Muslims out of Greece. Andifli's Greek community left for Greece. Kastellorizo itself stayed Greek, because Italy held the island then, but it lost the mainland markets it depended on and most of its people emigrated. Today a ferry crosses in about twenty minutes, and Greeks still come over for the Friday market. Two communities that were one, divided by a treaty neither of them wrote. Hold that thought; you meet it again at sunset.

The harbour is free to wander; boat trips are not, and prices are in lira (₺). Agree the price and what it includes before you step aboard, and verify it at the kiosk — nothing here is fixed. Now walk west along the waterfront and follow the signs for the antik tiyatro, the ancient theatre.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to wander the harbour. Boat trips, dives and the ferry to Meis are charged separately — agree the price and inclusions before you book, and verify at the kiosk.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Boat and dive kiosks along the harbour generally operate through the day in season (roughly April to October).
stops.accessibility: Level, paved waterfront, step-free along the quay. Boarding a boat needs a step or a gangway — ask the crew for a hand.
stops.insiderTip: Check the water before you book a boat: after a windy night it turns murky, and the clearest days are the calm ones. And photograph the boats, not the crews — if you want a portrait, ask first.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the harbour and walk west along the waterfront, then follow the signs uphill for the antik tiyatro. It is about a ten-minute climb on stepped lanes; the theatre opens up ahead of you, facing the sea.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Antiphellos Ancient Theatre
stops.narration:
You have climbed a few hundred metres from the harbour and the town has opened out below you. This is the theatre of Antiphellos, and it is the only ancient theatre in all of Anatolia that faces the sea. That is not a small claim: Anatolia — Asian Turkey — is littered with Greek and Roman theatres, and almost all of them were built into hillsides facing inland, away from the water. This one looks straight out at the island of Meis and the open Mediterranean.

Look at the shape. It seated about four thousand people, cut into the slope in a curve a little more than a semicircle, with the rows of seats carried on a retaining wall of irregular ashlar blocks — squared stones laid in courses, cut to fit each other rather than to one uniform size. Two things are missing. There is no diazoma, the walkway that normally divides the lower seats from the upper in a large theatre, and there is no permanent stone stage building, the skene. Scholars think the stage was left out on purpose so that nothing would block the view of the sea. Imagine the performance: a tragedy by Euripides with the actual Aegean as the backdrop — either the best or the worst staging decision in antiquity, depending on the play.

The period word is Hellenistic — the centuries after Alexander the Great, roughly 323 to 31 BC, when Greek language and building spread across the eastern Mediterranean. Antiphellos was by then a Lycian town that had gone thoroughly Greek; the Lycian language disappears from its coins and inscriptions around 200 BC. The Lycians (Likya in Turkish) were not Greeks at all — they were an Anatolian people with their own Indo-European language and alphabet — but their cities had joined the Lycian League, a federation with proportional voting that is one of the earliest experiments in representative government anywhere.

Now notice the repair. The east wall of this theatre collapsed at some point, most likely in the great Lycian earthquake of 141 AD, which also sent a tsunami along this coast and — as you hear on the boat trip — helped sink the town at Kekova. The wall was rebuilt soon afterwards, probably with money given to the city by Opramoas of Rhodiapolis, a fabulously rich civic benefactor who funded rebuilding across Lycia. Ancient cities ran on private philanthropy dressed up as public virtue.

The theatre was restored in 2008 and is used again for concerts and a jazz festival — a good outcome, because a theatre that is used is a theatre that is maintained. Entry is free and it is generally open at all hours; verify locally, since events sometimes close the seating. Wear shoes with grip: the stone rows are worn smooth, and the steps between them are steep and uneven. Now walk back down into the shopping lanes.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, with open access. Occasional concerts and festivals close the seating — verify locally on the day.
stops.openingHours: Generally open access at all times. Events, rehearsals and restoration occasionally close it — confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free. The theatre is up a stepped climb of several minutes, and the seating rows themselves are steep, worn stone. The view from the top of the lane is good even if you do not go down into the rows.
stops.insiderTip: Come back for a concert if the season offers one — the theatre hosts a jazz festival, and hearing live music in a two-thousand-year-old, sea-facing auditorium beats any museum case.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down into the town centre and find Uzunçarşı Caddesi, the long market street lined with shops. Walk east along it for about ten minutes; the Lycian tomb stands in the middle of the lane, impossible to miss once you know it is a tomb.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: rheins, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: King's Tomb (Lycian Mausoleum)
stops.narration:
Stop in the middle of the street. You are looking at a Lycian tomb — and it stands exactly where it was built, in the middle of a shopping lane, which tells you how the Lycians treated their dead. Locals call it the King's Tomb, Kral Mezarı; no king is buried here, as far as anyone knows. It is a mausoleum from the fourth century BC: a sarcophagus — a stone coffin, from the Greek for "flesh-eating" — sitting on top of a hyposorium, a burial chamber cut from the living rock below. The lid carries two projecting lions' heads and four panels of standing figures in relief. Look at the front pediment, the triangular face beneath the lid: a bearded man leaning on a staff beside a seated woman. Most scholars read them as the tomb's builder and his wife, watching the street for two and a half thousand years.

The inscription is why this tomb is famous. It is carved in Milyan, also called Lycian B — an extinct Anatolian language attested on only three inscriptions in the world: two poems on the obelisk at Xanthos, and this one. It is not a standard epitaph. When the British archaeologist Charles Fellows copied it in the 1840s he noted, with some surprise, that it contains no funereal words at all and reads like a poem. The text has never been convincingly translated. You are looking at a sentence in a dead language that nobody on earth can currently read.

Now the bigger picture. The Lycians buried their dead in the middle of life. Sarcophagi stand in streets and gardens; other tombs are cut into the cliff faces above the town. The usual explanation for the high rock tombs is a belief that a winged creature would carry the dead onward, and that it helped to start from high ground; the belief is reported rather than proven, but the effect is unmistakable — this is a town that has always lived among its ancestors. Most of Antiphellos's tombs are gone, by the way. In the nineteenth century people used the flat, cut stones as building material, and the ancient city was quarried into the modern one. This survivor, on Uzunçarşı Caddesi — "long market street", nicknamed slippery street after rain — is the best of what is left.

The tomb is free to see, on the street, at any hour. Treat it as a grave, because it is one: no climbing, no leaning, no sitting on the lid. Then walk south, downhill, toward the water.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It stands on a public street and can be viewed at any hour. Treat it as a grave — do not climb on or lean against the stonework.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times; it is a monument on a public shopping street.
stops.accessibility: Viewed from the street, so no steps are needed to see it. The lane itself is cobbled, uneven and slopes downhill, and can be slick after rain.
stops.insiderTip: Bring your eyes, not your hands. Read the inscription from the street and leave the stone alone — it is one of only three texts in its language anywhere in the world.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue south down Uzunçarşı and the lanes beyond it, toward the water. In a few minutes you reach the small pebble cove of Küçük Çakıl, tucked below the road on your left.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Küçük Çakıl Pebble Cove
stops.narration:
Here is the swim. This is Küçük Çakıl — "little pebble" — one of the small coves that hang off the town, and the first thing to understand is that Kaş has almost no sand. The coast is limestone and there are no large rivers to grind rock into sand and dump it on the shore, so the beaches are made of pebbles and shingle: smooth grey and white stones, hot underfoot at midday. That is not a defect. Pebble beaches mean clear water, because there is no sand stirred up in the swell.

The water gets deep quickly — a few steps and you are out of your depth — which is wonderful for swimming and worth knowing if you have small children or are a weak swimmer. The clarity you saw from the harbour holds up close: on a calm day you can see the bottom several metres down, and the sea runs from turquoise to a deep blue where the limestone drops away. Late-September water is usually in the mid-twenties Celsius, warm enough to stay in without braving anything.

Two things live here that you should know about. The first is the loggerhead sea turtle, Caretta caretta — a large marine turtle with a reddish-brown shell and an oversized head, which nests on beaches along this coast and is often seen swimming offshore. If you meet one, keep your distance and do not touch or chase it; they are protected, and a frightened turtle wastes energy it needs. The second is the sea urchin, a black spiny ball that lives on the rocks; wear sandals or water shoes near the rocky edges, and if you do step on one, do not dig the spines out with a needle — get help from a pharmacist.

The coves are free to use; operators charge for a sunbed and umbrella, and there is usually a small café. There may be no lifeguard, so swim within your ability and never alone. And respect the people around you: this is a public beach, not a photo set, so keep the camera off strangers — no pictures of bathers, ever. The town's own beaches are pebble; if you want the famous sand-and-gorge photograph, Kaputaş is twenty kilometres west and is a day trip, not a stroll.

Dry off, put your shoes back on, and walk west along the coast road to the peninsula.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to use the cove. Sunbeds and umbrellas, where offered, are charged by the operator; the café is at menu prices.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Café and sunbed service run through the day in season; the beach is best in the early morning or late afternoon.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free. A short sloping path and a few steps lead down to the shingle, and pebbles are loose underfoot. No step-free access to the water.
stops.insiderTip: Swim in the early morning or late afternoon, when the stones are cool and locals swim. Midday pebbles are genuinely too hot for bare feet — bring sandals.
stops.nextStopDirections: Climb back to the coast road and walk west, following the shoreline around the neck of the peninsula. Fifteen to twenty minutes of level walking brings you to the open western side and the sunset viewpoint over the bay.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: HALUK COMERTEL, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Çukurbağ Peninsula
stops.narration:
Cross the neck of land west of town and you are on the peninsula — the Yarımada, or Çukurbağ, the headland that curves out into the bay and gives Kaş its shape. Come here for the last hour of daylight. In autumn the sun sets over the water on this side, and from the near end of the peninsula you get the whole picture at once: the town on its little headland, the bay, the mountains of the Lycian coast behind you, and Meis out to the south.

Look up at the ridge. Locals call it the Sleeping Giant, Uyuyan Dev — a rocky profile in the cliff line that, from the right angle, reads as a figure lying on its back. It is a good example of how people make landmarks out of geology, and it is also a serious walk: the direct way up from town is steep and loose, and the safer approach is a long loop from the east. Not today. Today you are here for the view, not the summit.

This peninsula is also where the town's argument about its own future is being had, in concrete. Until the 1990s Kaş was a quiet fishing and sponge-diving town; tourism took off in that decade, at first mostly British and German visitors, and the growth spilled onto this headland — hotels and apartment blocks, some of them built without proper permission, pressing onto a coast that is both beautiful and fragile. You can see both sides from here. The building is income: hotels and restaurants employ the town, and the season is short. The building is also the thing that eats the reason people come. Residents and environmental groups have fought over it for years; the state has protected parts of this coast and lost other arguments. Stand here and you are watching a town decide what it wants to be.

The peninsula is a working neighbourhood, not just a viewpoint — people live out here, dolmuş minibuses run along the road, and the ride out costs a few tens of lira; ask the driver the price before you board, since it changes. The Lycian Way, Turkey's long-distance coastal footpath, crosses this headland, and above the village of Çukurbağ lie the ruins of Phellos — the inland city that Antiphellos was the port for. That is a separate expedition on a separate day, not a detour from sunset.

Stay until the light goes, then turn back toward the harbour. As the town's lights come on, so do the lights across the water.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free viewpoint and open road. A dolmuş minibus out here costs a few tens of lira — about 50 ₺ as of 2025, but ask the driver, since fares change.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times; best in the hour before sunset. Dolmuş minibuses run through the day and stop earlier in the evening — check the last one.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level along the peninsula road, with kerbs and some unpaved edges. The best viewpoints sit close to the road; the ridge path up the Sleeping Giant is steep and not for everyone.
stops.insiderTip: Stay for the ten minutes after the sun goes down, not just the moment of sunset — the afterglow over Meis is the best part, and the crowd leaves early.
stops.nextStopDirections: When the light goes, walk back east along the peninsula road the way you came, then follow the waterfront around the headland into town. The harbour front and its restaurants are ahead of you; the walk back takes about fifteen minutes.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Alexkom000, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Harbour Front
stops.narration:
Back where you started, and the harbour has changed costume. The boats are dark, the water has gone from turquoise to ink, and the front is filling with people doing the thing this town does best: eating late, slowly, at tables a metre from the sea. This is the last stop, so sit down if you can and let the walk settle.

Order the way the coast does. Meze are the small plates — the word simply means "appetiser" — brought out in a run of cold and warm dishes: stuffed vine leaves, puréed aubergine, octopus, white cheese, whatever the kitchen has. With them comes rakı, the aniseed spirit that turns milky the moment you add water, and which people here drink slowly with food and conversation, never in shots. Fish is usually priced by the kilo; ask the price before it is cooked, which is normal here, not rude. Everything is in lira, written ₺, and if you are used to euros the numbers will look alarming and the bill will not.

Look back at what you walked. You started among working boats in a harbour that has been a harbour since the Lycians, climbed to a Greek theatre that stares at the sea, stood in a shopping street beside a tomb with an unreadable poem on it, swam in a pebble cove, and watched the sun drop behind the peninsula while a Greek island floated two kilometres away. The town you walked is Antiphellos, Andifli and Kaş, layered on top of one another — Lycian, Greek, Roman, Ottoman, Turkish — and it wears all of it lightly, which is the most attractive thing about it.

Your two other days are already spoken for, and they are good promises. Kaputaş beach, twenty kilometres west, is the postcard: a sliver of pale shingle at the bottom of a gorge, reached by about 170 steps down from the coast road, with deep water, a small café and turtles offshore — go early, the car park is tiny and the steps are the whole point. Kekova, east along the coast, is the other one: kayak or sail over the ruins of a town sunk by the earthquake of the second century AD, with swimming and diving forbidden over the sunken part itself, so the stones stay where the sea put them. And Meis is a twenty-minute ferry away if you carry your passport.

If you have an evening left after all that, come back to this harbour front. It is free, it is open, and it is the one place in town that shows you everything at once: the boats, the bay, the island, and the lights of a country that used to be the same country as this one.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the front. Food, drink and the ferry to Meis are at menu and operator prices — ask for fish by the kilo and the price before it is cooked.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Restaurants and bars along the front run late through the season (roughly April to October).
stops.accessibility: Level, paved waterfront, step-free along the quay. Restaurant terraces often have a step or two up from the pavement.
stops.insiderTip: Ask for the fish by the kilo and the price before it is cooked — that is how it is done here. Then look south for the lights of Meis: another country, two kilometres away.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Stroll either way along the harbour front — cafés, tea and taxis line the quay. Kaputaş, Kekova and the Meis ferry all leave from the harbour, and the town centre is a couple of minutes inland.
